feedback: If a child believes rings belong to Saturn alone as the only ringed planet: Saturn's rings are the brightest and most obvious, but all four giant outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) have ring systems.
If the hottest-planet answer is Mercury: distance from the Sun is not the only factor — Venus's thick atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than closer Mercury.
Confirm a correct 'why is Mars red' choice by restating that the red is rust (iron oxide) in the rocks, not heat.
activities.intendedInsight: Distinctive features stay attached to the correct planet rather than blurring into a single list of names.
learnerActions: Match each feature to its planet: rings → Saturn, Great Red Spot → Jupiter, red/rust → Mars, tilted on its side → Uranus, smallest and closest → Mercury, hottest → Venus, farthest and very cold → Neptune.
Answer: 'Which planet is the hottest?' — choosing from options that include the tempting Mercury (closest) distractor.
Answer: 'Why is Mars red?' — choosing rust/iron oxide rather than heat or fire.
State one distinctive feature for at least six of the eight planets in your own words.
activities.title: Match the Feature to the Right Planet

feedback: Full understanding: the child explains Venus is hottest because its thick atmosphere traps heat while Mercury's escapes, names features for several planets, and attributes Mars's red to rust rather than heat.
Partial: the child accepts Venus is hottest and names features but cannot say WHY an atmosphere makes the difference — introduce the atmosphere-as-blanket idea explicitly.
Gap: the child insists Mercury must be hottest (running distance as the only factor) or ties Mars's colour to heat — reteach the trapping-heat idea and separate colour (rust) from temperature.
activities.intendedInsight: A planet's temperature is shaped by its atmosphere as well as its distance from the Sun; the 'closer = hotter' rule alone cannot explain Venus.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'Mercury is closest to the Sun, so you might expect it to be hottest. But Venus is hotter than Mercury. How can a planet that is further from the Sun end up hotter? Tell me WHY.'

Explain in your own words that Venus's thick atmosphere of gases traps the Sun's heat like a blanket and lets it escape only very slowly, while Mercury has almost no atmosphere so its heat leaks away.

Consider follow-up questions: What does a thick atmosphere do to the heat a planet gets? Which matters more for how hot a planet is — only distance, or atmosphere too? If Mars is red because of rust, does that tell us it is hot, or something else? Why can't Jupiter's Great Red Spot be a mark painted on the ground?
activities.title: Explain the Puzzle: Why Is Venus Hotter?
